title: Air France Extends Dubai and Riyadh Flight Suspensions as Gulf Aviation Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Dozens of international airlines have scrapped planned returns to the Middle East, with British Airways delaying its Gulf restart to October and Finnair dropping Doha for the entire winter season.
body:
Air France has extended the suspension of its flights to Dubai and Riyadh, joining a growing list of international carriers that have scrapped planned returns to the Gulf as the US-Iran conflict continues to disrupt commercial aviation across the Middle East.

The French flag carrier had scheduled a July 20 resumption of its Middle East network, but scrapped the restart as conditions deteriorated. Flights to Dubai International Airport — the world's busiest by international passengers — will remain grounded until July 27, while Riyadh services stay suspended until July 24. Air France also pushed back its Beirut resumption to August 2.

European Carriers Pull Back From the Gulf

Air France's decision follows the European Union Aviation Safety Agency extending its advisory urging airlines to avoid or exercise extreme caution over Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE, and the Gulf of Oman until July 29, citing escalating military activity between the US and Iran.

The advisory has triggered cascading schedule changes across European carriers. British Airways has pushed its planned return to Dubai, Tel Aviv, Bahrain, and Amman to October 25 — nearly four months away — and permanently suspended its Jeddah route. When Gulf services do resume, frequencies will be sharply reduced: Doha flights drop from twice daily to once daily starting August 1, while Riyadh cuts from two daily to one from August 8.

KLM has suspended Riyadh, Dammam, and Dubai flights until August 23, rerouting remaining flights around Iranian, Iraqi, and Israeli airspace. Lufthansa Group has suspended Dubai services until September 13, with its subsidiaries Swiss, Austrian Airlines, and Brussels Airlines keeping routes to Abu Dhabi, Riyadh, Beirut, and several other Middle Eastern cities on hold until October 24.

Finnair has extended its Helsinki-Dubai suspension to October 24 and dropped Doha for the entire winter season, rerouting passengers onto Qatar Airways-operated flights through March 2027.

Asian Carriers Follow Suit

The disruption extends well beyond Europe. Singapore Airlines, which had planned an August 2 return to Dubai, has pushed its suspension to October 24, warning that "the situation remains fluid" and other flights may be affected. Cathay Pacific has extended its Dubai and Riyadh suspensions to late October, while Philippine Airlines has suspended Dubai until October 2.

Air Canada has pushed its Dubai and Tel Aviv suspensions through early September, and Air Astana has grounded its UAE flights until August 31, citing the "deterioration of the situation in the Strait of Hormuz."

Gulf Carriers Project Confidence Despite Disruptions

Middle Eastern carriers themselves are projecting a more resilient picture. At the Farnborough Airshow on Tuesday, Emirates President Tim Clark told Reuters that the airline was "flying at 90% capacity" with full premium cabins, despite the conflict.

"I think the closer you are to the centre of the Gulf operation, the more normal you realise things are."

— Paul Griffiths, CEO, Dubai Airports

Clark urged the industry to "think positive, act positive, be positive" about the region's recovery, even as Air France-KLM — one of Europe's largest airline groups — extended its suspensions. Turkish Airlines has resumed flights to Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Damascus, Beirut, and Amman, though its Iran routes remain suspended.

Impact on Indian Diaspora Travel

The suspensions hit Gulf hubs that serve as critical connecting points for flights between India, Europe, and North America. Dubai and Doha handle millions of Indian passengers annually, and reduced frequencies or outright cancellations through the coming months will shrink seat availability and raise fares on routes that Indian travelers depend on.

Direct India-Europe flights on carriers not transiting Gulf airspace become more valuable as alternatives, though capacity on those routes is limited. Indian carriers with Gulf exposure — including Air India and IndiGo, which operate extensive Middle East networks — face their own operational decisions as the conflict evolves.

All affected airlines are offering free rebooking or full refunds for impacted passengers. Air France said travelers who booked directly can adjust plans through its My Bookings portal, while those who booked through agencies should contact their original point of sale.
